planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Augustus was selected for its broad, folded leaves and unusually rounded, chunky flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Augustus is a Galanthus plicatus selection named by the English plantsman E.A. Bowles, distinguished by wide, strap-shaped, folded-margin leaves and unusually rounded, almost globular flowers that open wider than many other snowdrops. It is a steady, undemanding grower that bulks up at a moderate pace into clumps worth dividing every few years. Lift and replant congested clumps immediately after flowering while the foliage is still green for best results.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Godfrey Owen is a poculiform snowdrop with six outer-sized petals instead of the usual three long and three short.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Godfrey Owen is a tall, vigorous poculiform snowdrop in which all six petals are enlarged and roughly equal in size, giving each flower a fuller, more symmetrical look than the typical three-long, three-short snowdrop shape. Named for a Shropshire plantsman, it increases at a good pace and is one of the more readily obtainable poculiform forms for gardeners wanting something distinctive without chasing ultra-rare named clones. Divide congested clumps right after flowering while leaves are still green.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Hippolyta is one of the Greatorex double snowdrops, bred mid-20th century in Norfolk and named for a Shakespearean character.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Hippolyta is one of the Greatorex double snowdrops bred in Norfolk, England, by Heyrick Greatorex in the mid-20th century, bearing a neat, fully double inner rosette of petals packed inside the outer segments for an unusually full flower. It is a reliable, moderately vigorous grower well suited to a woodland or shaded border planting alongside other hellebores and early bulbs. Lift and divide crowded clumps in the green immediately after flowering for the best transplant success.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jaquenetta is another of Heyrick Greatorex's Shakespeare-named double snowdrops.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Jaquenetta, named after a character from Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost, is one of the Greatorex double snowdrops raised in Norfolk in the mid-20th century, producing a tidy, well-filled double flower on sturdy stems. It clumps up steadily and makes an easy, long-lived addition to a shaded border or woodland garden once established. Divide congested clumps in the green right after flowering for best results.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dionysus is a vigorous, large-flowered Greatorex double snowdrop.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Dionysus is one of the larger-flowered Greatorex double snowdrops bred in Norfolk in the mid-20th century, with broad outer petals surrounding a generously filled double center that gives the bloom extra heft compared to many other doubles. It is a dependable, fairly vigorous grower that forms worthwhile clumps within a few seasons. Divide congested clumps in the green immediately after flowering while foliage is still active.

common_name: Blewbury Tart Snowdrop (Spiky Green-Marked Poculiform Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blewbury Tart is a strikingly irregular poculiform snowdrop with narrow, green-marked petals in a starry, untidy arrangement.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Named for the Oxfordshire village of Blewbury, this poculiform snowdrop has an irregular, starry arrangement of narrow petals heavily brushed with green, giving each flower a distinctly untidy, almost shaggy look compared to a classic snowdrop. It is a conversation-piece cultivar prized by collectors for that very oddity, and it increases at a modest but steady rate once settled. Divide clumps in the green just after flowering for the best transplant success.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Straffan is one of the oldest named snowdrop cultivars, traced back to Straffan House in County Kildare, Ireland.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Straffan is among the earliest-recorded named snowdrop cultivars, tracing back to the grounds of Straffan House in County Kildare, Ireland, and valued for its neat, rounded flowers and reliable early-season bloom. It is a slow but steady increaser, making it a good choice for collectors wanting a direct link to the earliest days of organized snowdrop naming. Lift and divide clumps in the green right after flowering to encourage faster bulking.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this naturally occurring form has a spathe that splits into two long, ear-like points above the flower.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Known informally as the donkey-eared snowdrop, this naturally occurring variant of the common snowdrop has a spathe, the thin papery sheath behind the flower, that splits into two elongated points standing up like a pair of ears, making it instantly recognizable even from a distance. Otherwise it behaves just like the common snowdrop, multiplying steadily by bulb offsets to form expanding drifts over time. Divide crowded clumps in the green immediately after flowering for quickest establishment.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Primrose Warburg has a yellow ovary and yellow-tinged inner petal markings rather than the usual green.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Named for the Oxford galanthophile Primrose Warburg, this cultivar replaces the usual green ovary and inner petal marks with soft yellow, giving the flower a warmer tone than most snowdrops, and it is notably more vigorous and easier to grow than many other yellow-toned forms. It bulks up at a good pace once established in a cool, humus-rich site. Divide congested clumps in the green right after flowering for best transplant success.

common_name: Spindlestone Surprise Snowdrop (Yellow Ovary and Pedicel Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this cultivar was found growing at Spindlestone in Northumberland and has yellow rather than green ovary, pedicel, and inner markings.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. First found growing at Spindlestone in Northumberland, this snowdrop carries yellow pigment through the ovary, flower stalk, and inner petal markings in place of the usual green, standing out clearly against the white outer petals. It grows a touch more slowly than many green-marked snowdrops, so give it an undisturbed spot with consistent moisture to help it settle in. Divide clumps in the green immediately after flowering once they are well established.

common_name: Hill Poe Snowdrop (Historic Irish Double Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Hill Poe is a historic double snowdrop named for James Hill Poe of Riverston, County Tipperary, Ireland.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Hill Poe is a long-established Irish double snowdrop, named for James Hill Poe of Riverston in County Tipperary, with rounded outer petals surrounding a neatly packed double center that gives the flower a plump, substantial look. It is a dependable, easy-going grower well suited to naturalizing in a woodland setting alongside other historic snowdrop cultivars. Divide congested clumps in the green right after flowering while leaves are still active.

common_name: Lady Beatrix Stanley Snowdrop (Rounded Historic Double Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Lady Beatrix Stanley bears neat, well-rounded double flowers and was named for a noted English gardener and galanthophile.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Lady Beatrix Stanley, named for the English gardener and early galanthophile of the same name, carries a tidy, well-formed double flower that keeps its neat rounded shape better than many other doubles as it ages on the plant. It is a vigorous, reliable grower that bulks up readily into generous clumps, making it one of the more widely available historic double snowdrop cultivars. Divide congested clumps in the green immediately after flowering for best transplant success.
